## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | The Khasi are an Austroasiatic ethnic group. |
| Where | Meghalaya in north-eastern India, with populations in Assam and parts of Bangladesh. |
| How many | Over 1.41 million Khasi lived in Meghalaya, 35 thousand in Assam, and around 85 thousand in Bangladesh’s Sylhet Division according to the 2011 Census of India. |
| Language | Khasi, an Austroasiatic language. |
| Religion | Indigenous Khasi religion, Ka Niam Khasi, is monotheistic; around 83.14% are Christian and 15.41% follow Ka Niam Khasi. |
| Known for | matrilineal society · distinctive dress · weaving · oral mythology · living root bridges |

## Overview

The Khasi live mainly in Meghalaya, especially the Khasi Hills and eastern Meghalaya. They are known for matrilineal society, weaving, distinctive dress, oral mythology, and living root bridges. Khasi is an Austroasiatic language written in the Latin script. Most Khasi people are Christian, while a smaller group follows Ka Niam Khasi.

## Material culture

Khasi material culture includes woven fabrics, ceremonial clothing, living root bridges, and tools and baskets recorded in museum collections.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Khasi textile traditions include Ryndia and Eri silk, with women central to Eri silk production.

- **Hand-woven fabric** (*Ryndia*) — Ryndia is a hand-spun, hand-woven fabric worn by men and women in undyed off-white or maroon and mustard plaid.
- **Peace silk** (*Eri silk*) — Eri silk is called “peace silk” because its production process is considered non-violent, and women do the weaving and production in Meghalaya.

### Clothing & dress

Traditional Khasi dress uses distinctive male and female garments, with more elaborate clothing worn on ceremonial occasions.

- **Sleeveless coat** (*Jymphong*) — The Jymphong is a longish sleeveless coat without a collar, fastened at the front with thongs.
- **Female garment** (*Jainsem*) — The Jainsem is an elaborate garment made from two pieces of material fastened at each shoulder.
- **Female garment** (*Dhara*) — The Dhara is an elaborate garment made from a single piece fastened at each shoulder.

### Architecture

The War inhabitants of the Khasi community built living root bridges in the War region.

- **Living root bridges** — Living root bridges were designed and built by the War inhabitants of the Khasi community in the War region.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Recorded Khasi objects include iron tools, bows, bamboo baskets, and a cane water-pipe.

- **Curved-blade bill** — A bill has a wide, curved iron blade and a carved wooden shaft.
- **Carrying basket** — A miniature bamboo carrying basket has a lid, wickerwork construction, a plaited bamboo strap, and three brown bamboo stripes.
- **Bow** — A bow is made of wood with a cane string and a metal sleeve.
- **Bill-hook** — A bill-hook has an iron blade, carved wooden haft, and plaited rattan.
- **Cane water-pipe** — The collection includes part of a cane water-pipe.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Ceremonial Khasi adornment includes crowns and ornamental waist-bands.

- **Ceremonial crown** — Women may wear ceremonial crowns of silver or gold with a spike or peak fixed to the back.
- **Ornamental waist-band** — Men may wear an ornamental waist-band with the Jymphong and sarong on ceremonial occasions.

## Music & performance

The profile names a Khasi folk singer and the Shillong Chamber Choir.

- **Khasi folk singer** — Skendrowell Syiemlieh is identified as a Khasi folk singer.
- **Choir** — The Shillong Chamber Choir is identified, but its repertoire and performance practice are not described.

## Festivals & rituals

Khasi mythology tells of seven families remaining on earth after the human race was divided into 16 heavenly families.

- **The Seven Huts** (*Ki Hynñiewtrep*) — Ki Hynñiewtrep is the name for the Khasi tribe’s original abode, meaning “The Seven Huts.”
- **God, the Lord Master** (*U Blei Trai Kynrad*) — U Blei Trai Kynrad distributed the human race into 16 heavenly families.
- **Sixteen heavenly families** (*Khadhynriew Trep*) — Khadhynriew Trep is the name for the 16 heavenly families, with seven families remaining on earth and nine in heaven.
- **Heavenly peak** (*Lum Sohpetbneng Peak*) — A heavenly ladder resting on Lum Sohpetbneng Peak once enabled people to travel freely to heaven.
- **Divine tree peak** (*Lum Diengiei Peak*) — Access to heaven ended after people were tricked into cutting a divine tree at Lum Diengiei Peak.

## Foodways

Khasi crops include fruits, nuts, rice, and vegetables.

- **Betel leaves** — Betel leaves are among the main crops produced by the Khasi.
- **Areca nut** — Areca nut is among the main crops produced by the Khasi.
- **Local varieties of rice** — Local varieties of rice are among the main crops produced by the Khasi.
- **Pineapples** — Pineapples are among the main crops produced by the Khasi.
- **Vegetables** — Vegetables are among the main crops produced by the Khasi.

## Oral tradition & literature

Khasi oral tradition includes mythology, fables, folk-tales, folk songs, and tales.

- **Khasi fables and folk-tales** — Khasi fables and folk-tales are documented literary materials and include a book by Hamlet Bareh.
- **Khasi Folk Tales** — Khasi Folk Tales is a book by Mrs. Rafy.
- **Khasi Folk Songs & Tales** — Khasi Folk Songs & Tales is a book by Desmond L. Kharmawphlang and A. R. Tripathi.

## Language & religion

Khasi is a matrilineal society’s Austroasiatic language, and its indigenous religion is monotheistic.

- **Indigenous Khasi religion** (*Ka Niam Khasi*) — Ka Niam Khasi is the indigenous Khasi religion.
- **Supreme creator** (*U Blei Nongthaw*) — U Blei Nongthaw is the one, formless supreme creator in Ka Niam Khasi.
- **Shillong Plateau language group** (*Khasic group*) — Pnar, Lyngngam, and War are identified as Khasi’s closest relatives in the Khasic group of the Shillong Plateau.
- **First Khasi publication** (*First Khasi Reader*) — The First Khasi Reader became one of the first Khasi publications in 1842.
- **Catechism** (*Rhodd Mam*) — Rhodd Mam became one of the first Khasi publications in 1842.

## Glossary

- *Ryndia* — hand-spun, hand-woven fabric
- *Eri silk* — peace silk
- *Jymphong* — traditional male garment
- *Jainsem* — female garment
- *Dhara* — female garment
- *Ki Hynñiewtrep* — The Seven Huts
- *U Blei Trai Kynrad* — God, the Lord Master
- *Khadhynriew Trep* — 16 heavenly families
- *Lum Sohpetbneng Peak* — site of the heavenly ladder
- *Lum Diengiei Peak* — site of the divine tree
- *Ka Niam Khasi* — indigenous Khasi religion
- *U Blei Nongthaw* — formless supreme creator
- *Khasic group* — language group of the Shillong Plateau
- *First Khasi Reader* — early Khasi publication
- *Rhodd Mam* — early Khasi catechism

## Sources & further reading

- Hamlet Bareh, *Khasi fables and folk-tales*, Firma K.L. Mukhopadhyay, 1971.
- Mrs. Rafy, *Khasi Folk Tales*, Cosmo Publications, 1987 [1929].
- Desmond L. Kharmawphlang and A. R. Tripathi, *Khasi Folk Songs & Tales*, Sahitya Akademi, 2006.
- Lili Rabel, *Khasi, a Language of Assam*, Louisiana State University Press, 1961.

- Khasi mythology: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khasi_mythology
- Khasi language: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khasi_language
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: the supplied sources identify no UNESCO ICH inscriptions for India concerning the Khasi.
- British Museum collections: https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection

commons_photos.title: Nongsawlia Presbyterian Church, East Khasi hills district, Meghalaya, India.jpg
commons_photos.description:
Nongsawlia Presbyterian Church, Nongsawlia, Sohra
The Nongsawlia Presbyterian Church is the first established Christian church in Meghalaya. It was established long back in the year 1846.
The first Church Building was built upon a hillock of the present Nongsawlia Cemetery. This building was destroyed by the great earthquake occurred in June 1897. The new Church Building at the present Site was built in 1898 i.e., a hundred years ago. The membership of the Nongsawlia Presbyterian Church had increased slowly and steadily. In 1847, there were five members, in 1848, there were 6 members including one young woman ka Nabon Sawian who was baptized in 14th July, 1848. She was the first woman to become Christian inspite of threatening and persecution from the family members. In 1853 the members increased to 24. From Nongsawlia as an origin of Christianity, the Presbyterian Church had spread to different parts of Khasi-Jaintia Hills, to Mawnai in 1854, to Jowai in 1858, to Shillong in 1871. The present statistic of the Presbyterian church in Khasi-Jaintia Hills is more than 5 lakhs.
The Presbyterian Church of Wales known at that time as the "The Calvinistic Methodist Church of Wales" sent the first Missionary to Khasi Hills, they are, Rev. Thomas Jones-I and his young Wife Anne Thomas. They left Wales in November 1840 and after five months they arrived at Calcutta. From Calcutta they travel by boat and landed at Majai, the southern part of Khasi Hills. From Majai they climbed up reaching Laittyra and finally arrived at Saitsohpen, Sohra (Cherrapunjee) on the 22nd, June, 1841 which is the Head Quarter of the then Sylhet Light Infantry, a force of Sepoy troops under the British command since 1835.From the Military and Government officials, Thomas Jones received cold reception. One British official advised Thomas Jones and said "go back home Jones; you may as well try to instruct the monkeys on that tree than to attempt to teach these people". They looked down the Khasi people as illiterate and ignorant. But Thomas Jones was not discouraged instead he bent down devoted heart and soul to do the work for which he had been called by God. By God's providence there was a devout Christian, Lieutenant William Lewin (1806-1846) who welcomed Thomas Jones and his wife and give them a shelter in one of his rooms in the White Bungalow at Saitsohpen. The kindness of William Lewin helped Thomas Jones and his wife to feel at home in a foreign land accompanied with heavy rainfall of 264 inches in the month of August alone.
In 1843 Thomas Jones moved to a new site at Nongsawlia, a plot of land given by the Chief of ka Hima Sohra (Cherra Syiemship), U Suba Syiem. At that time there were five Missionaries, Thomas Jones, Mrs. Jones, Rev. William Lewis, Mrs. William Lewis and Dr. Richard. At this new station the Missionaries had built two Bungalows, School and the Church building.
Thomas Jones from the beginning devoted his time listening attentively the pronunciation of the Khasi words and learnt the language. It is said that only in 7/8 months he could converse with people and preached the Gospel. He rejected the Bengalee scripts and adopted the Roman scripts A, B, K, D etc. He opened three schools at Mawsmai, Mawmluh and Sohra. He wrote the first Reader and the second Reader using the Roman scripts to be taught in these Schools. Thomas Jones was successful in his attempt, and Hence, Thomas Jones was known as the Father of the Khasi Alphabets and also the founder of the khasi Literature. Nearly 5 (five) years had passed since the coming of the first missionary from Wales, Rev. and Mrs. Thomas Jones but no one from among the Khasis responded to the preaching of the Gospel. "It was till the 8th of March 1846 that the first two khasis" U Amor and U Rujon were baptized by the Rev. William Lewis. "This event marked the beginning of the Presbyterian Church at Nongsawlia and indeed the Presbyterian Church in the Khasi-Jaintia Hills".

Description credit to Sohra Civil Sub division, Sohra, East Khasi Hills district, Meghalaya, India.
